How far the held-out points sit from the training data

Source: R/fold-separation.R
fold_separation.Rd

Blocked cross-validation exists to put distance between a test point and the training points that could tell you its value. Whether it succeeded is a measurement, and make_folds() only offers a proxy for it: the block size compared against the estimated autocorrelation range, reported as a warning. That comparison is about the design. This is about the result: for every held-out point, the distance to its nearest training point, summarised per fold.

Usage

fold_separation(folds, data_sf, sac = NULL, prediction_points = NULL)

Arguments

folds

A make_folds() result, or its $folds element (a list of train/test splits).

data_sf

The layer the folds were built on. Row identifiers are matched through ..row_id when the layer carries one, and by row position otherwise, which is what make_folds() and every cv_*() do. As in cv_*(), a make_folds() result whose recorded rows sit at other locations here (folds built on another layer, such as the points before assign_features_to_polygons() dropped some) is refused; the location check is skipped when one of the two layers is POINT and the other is not.

sac

Optional: an estimate_sac_range() result or a single number. Defaults to the range the folds carry, if any. Supplying one adds the mean_cor column and, with a prediction target, the gap on the correlation scale. A range that records its CRS (the folds' own, or an estimate_sac_range() result) is compared with distances measured in that CRS, whatever CRS data_sf is in. A bare number is taken to be in the units the distances are otherwise measured in: those of data_sf if it is projected, and for geographic (lon/lat) input metres, in the CRS ensure_projected() chooses (as for make_folds()'s block_size), not degrees. A units object is refused.

prediction_points

Optional sf or sfc layer of the locations the model will predict at: the grid from predict_surface(), or a grid over the region of interest (sf::st_make_grid(region, what = "centers")). A non-POINT layer is reduced to one representative point per feature, as in make_folds(method = "nndm"), so pass grid cells or points, not one polygon of the region. It is brought into the CRS the distances are measured in. Default NULL: no target and no reading, except for NNDM and kNNDM folds (method = "nndm" and "knndm"), which carry the distances from the prediction points they were built for and are compared against those, measured to all sites. The carried distances are lengths in the CRS the folds were built in (folds$params$crs). When the distances here are measured in another CRS (data_sf is in another projected CRS, or sac records another), the two are not compared, print() says so, and passing prediction_points has the target measured here.

Value

A data.frame of class fold_separation, one row per fold: fold (the fold's number: for the $folds of a cv_*() result, the fold_id its fold_metrics use, which differs from the list position once a fold has been dropped), n_train, n_test, n_blocks (NA for a scheme with no blocks), min_dist and median_dist (distance from a held-out point to its nearest training point, in the units of the CRS the crs attribute names), mean_cor, target_median_dist (the median distance from the prediction points to the fold's training data) and dist_gap (the fold's mean held-out distance minus its mean prediction distance); the last two are NA without a target, and print() shows them under the headings target and gap.

mean_cor is a mean correlation, NA without a range: the mean over the fold's held-out points of \(\rho(d)\), the correlation the range leaves between a point and its nearest training point at distance \(d\). It is 1 for a point on top of training data and falls towards 0 beyond the range, so a point at a twentieth of the range counts for more than one at nine tenths of it. \(\rho(d)\) is \(\exp(-3 d / range)\), the exponential model whose effective range is the range given (0.05 at the range), or the spherical model when the range comes from an estimate_sac_range() fit that was spherical; the range_model attribute says which. Earlier development versions had a column within_range in its place: the share of held-out points closer than the range, which counted every such point the same.

Attributes: method, sac_range, range_model, crs (the CRS the distances were measured in), n_unknown_ids (the number of distinct rows the folds name that data_sf does not have, each counted once however many folds mention it, as in the cv_*() field of the same name), pooled (a list with the number, minimum, median and mean of the held-out distances over all folds, and the pooled mean_cor) and target: NULL without a prediction target, otherwise a list with n_prediction_points, source, basis ("each fold's training data" or "all sites"), held_out_mean, held_out_median, target_mean, target_median, target_all_mean, target_all_median (the prediction distances to all sites), mean_diff, w1, cor_gap, cor_w1 (NA without a range), scale ("correlation" or "distance"), tolerance, reading (see Reading the gap) and nndm_out_of_reach (for NNDM and kNNDM folds, the params$target_out_of_reach that make_folds() recorded; NA for other schemes). not_compared is NULL, or, for NNDM or kNNDM folds whose carried target was not compared because the distances here are measured in another CRS, one sentence naming the two CRSs; target is then NULL and print() gives the sentence where it would otherwise say that no target is given.

Details

The distances do not say by themselves which way a score errs. A cross-validated error reads low when the held-out points sit closer to their training data than the locations the model will predict at, and high when they sit farther, so the same held-out distances can go with either, depending on the target. Random folds on evenly sited data, scored for a map of the sampled area, are close to unbiased although nearly every held-out point has a training neighbour inside the range; range-sized blocks on the same data read high; random folds on clustered data scored for a map of the whole region read low. So without a prediction target the function reports the distances and draws no conclusion. Give it prediction_points and it sets the held-out distances beside the distances from those points to the same training data, and words its reading by the signed gap between the two.

Nothing is estimated: the distances come from the geometry, and the range, when one is shown, is the one the folds already carry (make_folds( auto_range = TRUE) records it) or the one you pass as sac.

Reading the gap

With a target, the held-out distances and the prediction distances are compared as two distributions. Each fold's prediction distances are measured to that fold's own training rows, so that a five-fold design is not read as too far only because each fold trains on four fifths of the sites; the distances to all sites are reported beside them. (With more than 50 folds, the leave-one-out schemes, every training set is nearly the whole sample and the prediction points are measured against all sites once.) Folds count by their share of the held-out points.

Two numbers summarise the comparison: the signed difference of the means, held-out minus prediction (the signed area between the two cumulative distributions), and the Wasserstein distance \(W_1\) (the unsigned area). When a range is available both are also given on the correlation scale, after each distance \(d\) is replaced by \(1 - \rho(d)\), with \(\rho\) the correlation the range implies (see mean_cor under Value). That scale counts a difference between two distances well inside the range and ignores one between two distances beyond it.

The reading is taken on the correlation scale when there is a range, with a tolerance of 0.1, and otherwise on the mean distance, with a tolerance of a quarter of the prediction mean. (When the prediction points are measured to all sites and every one lies on a site, as when the sites themselves are passed as prediction_points to a leave-one-out design, the prediction mean and with it that tolerance are 0: held-out distances above 0 then read "farther", and held-out distances that are all 0 as well read "matched". With 50 folds or fewer the points are measured to each fold's own training rows, which leave out that fold's held-out sites, so the mean is above 0 and the quarter rule gives the reading.)

"closer"

The gap is below minus the tolerance and at least half of \(W_1\) in size: the held-out points sit closer to their training data than the prediction points do, and the cross-validated error tends to read low for that target.

"farther"

The gap is above the tolerance and at least half of \(W_1\): the held-out points sit farther, and the error tends to read high.

"matched"

The gap is within the tolerance and \(W_1\) within twice the tolerance.

"mixed"

The two distributions cross, closer at some distances and farther at others (the gap is under half of \(W_1\), or it is within the tolerance while \(W_1\) is not), so the distances give no single direction.

The reading is a statement about nearest-neighbour distances, not a measured bias. A learner that draws on several neighbours can still score low on clustered samples whose nearest-neighbour distances match.

See also

make_folds() for the fold schemes and the block sizing this measures the outcome of; cv_block_size_sweep() for choosing a block size by cross-validated error instead.

Other cross-validation: area_of_applicability(), cv_bayes(), cv_block_size_sweep(), cv_gwr(), cv_rf(), cv_spatial(), estimate_sac_range(), gwr_model_selection(), make_folds(), sac_nugget(), select_features_forward()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)

# Random folds put a training point close to every held-out one.
random  <- make_folds(pts, k = 4, method = "random_kfold", seed = 1)
print(fold_separation(random, pts, sac = 200))
#> Fold separation: random_kfold, 4 fold(s), 200 held-out point(s) (EPSG:32632)
#>   autocorrelation range: 200 (in metres, like the distances)
#> 
#>  fold n_train n_test min_dist median_dist mean_cor
#>     1     150     50    4.696       36.95     0.57
#>     2     150     50    3.835       42.14     0.55
#>     3     150     50    3.835       38.52     0.58
#>     4     150     50    4.696       45.79     0.53
#> 
#>   Held-out points sit a median of 41.61 from their nearest training
#>   point; the closest is 3.835 away. Under the range of 200 that leaves a
#>   mean correlation of 0.56 between a held-out point and its nearest
#>   training point (exp(-3 d / range) averaged over the hold-out: 1 at
#>   distance 0, 0.05 at the range).
#>   No prediction target is given, so these are distances and no conclusion
#>   about the score: a cross-validated error reads low when the hold-out
#>   sits closer to its training data than the locations to be predicted do,
#>   and high when it sits farther. Pass `prediction_points` to compare the
#>   two.

# Blocked folds hold out whole neighbourhoods, so the distances grow.
blocked <- make_folds(pts, k = 4, method = "block_kfold",
                      block_size = 250, seed = 1)
print(fold_separation(blocked, pts, sac = 200))
#> Fold separation: block_kfold, 4 fold(s), 200 held-out point(s) (EPSG:32632)
#>   autocorrelation range: 200 (in metres, like the distances)
#> 
#>  fold n_train n_test n_blocks min_dist median_dist mean_cor
#>     1     152     48        2    23.02       111.9     0.23
#>     2     143     57        3    29.04       169.5     0.14
#>     3     152     48        2    21.03       118.3     0.22
#>     4     153     47        2    21.03       115.9     0.23
#> 
#>   Held-out points sit a median of 123.5 from their nearest training
#>   point; the closest is 21.03 away. Under the range of 200 that leaves a
#>   mean correlation of 0.20 between a held-out point and its nearest
#>   training point (exp(-3 d / range) averaged over the hold-out: 1 at
#>   distance 0, 0.05 at the range).
#>   No prediction target is given, so these are distances and no conclusion
#>   about the score: a cross-validated error reads low when the hold-out
#>   sits closer to its training data than the locations to be predicted do,
#>   and high when it sits farther. Pass `prediction_points` to compare the
#>   two.

# Which of the two suits a map of the sampled square?  Compare each with
# the distances from the cells of that map to the training data.
cells <- st_make_grid(pts, n = c(20, 20), what = "centers")
print(fold_separation(random, pts, sac = 200, prediction_points = cells))
#> Fold separation: random_kfold, 4 fold(s), 200 held-out point(s) (EPSG:32632)
#>   autocorrelation range: 200 (in metres, like the distances)
#>   prediction target: 400 point(s), measured to each fold's training data
#> 
#>  fold n_train n_test min_dist median_dist target     gap mean_cor
#>     1     150     50    4.696       36.95  37.82 -0.9056     0.57
#>     2     150     50    3.835       42.14  38.02  0.2229     0.55
#>     3     150     50    3.835       38.52  36.00 -1.8310     0.58
#>     4     150     50    4.696       45.79  37.28  3.9360     0.53
#> 
#>   Held-out points sit a median of 41.61 from their nearest training
#>   point; the closest is 3.835 away. Under the range of 200 that leaves a
#>   mean correlation of 0.56 between a held-out point and its nearest
#>   training point (exp(-3 d / range) averaged over the hold-out: 1 at
#>   distance 0, 0.05 at the range).
#>   The prediction points sit a median of 37.48 from the same training data
#>   (32.16 from the nearest of all sites). Held-out minus prediction:
#>   +0.3554 in mean distance (W1 3.371); +0.01 on the correlation scale (W1
#>   0.02). The held-out points sit about as far from their training data as
#>   the prediction points do. Matched nearest-neighbour distances do not
#>   make a score unbiased by themselves: a learner that draws on several
#>   neighbours can still read low on clustered samples.
print(fold_separation(blocked, pts, sac = 200, prediction_points = cells))
#> Fold separation: block_kfold, 4 fold(s), 200 held-out point(s) (EPSG:32632)
#>   autocorrelation range: 200 (in metres, like the distances)
#>   prediction target: 400 point(s), measured to each fold's training data
#> 
#>  fold n_train n_test n_blocks min_dist median_dist target   gap mean_cor
#>     1     152     48        2    23.02       111.9  39.37 58.97     0.23
#>     2     143     57        3    29.04       169.5  44.55 89.14     0.14
#>     3     152     48        2    21.03       118.3  40.95 65.42     0.22
#>     4     153     47        2    21.03       115.9  38.61 67.19     0.23
#> 
#>   Held-out points sit a median of 123.5 from their nearest training
#>   point; the closest is 21.03 away. Under the range of 200 that leaves a
#>   mean correlation of 0.20 between a held-out point and its nearest
#>   training point (exp(-3 d / range) averaged over the hold-out: 1 at
#>   distance 0, 0.05 at the range).
#>   The prediction points sit a median of 40.55 from the same training data
#>   (32.16 from the nearest of all sites). Held-out minus prediction:
#>   +71.05 in mean distance (W1 71.15); +0.30 on the correlation scale (W1
#>   0.30). The held-out points sit farther from their training data than
#>   the prediction points do, so the cross-validated error tends to read
#>   high for these prediction points.
